description_full: TSS, Inc. engages in the planning, design, deployment, maintenance, and refresh of end-user and enterprise systems in the United States. The company operates through three segments: Procurement, Facilities Management, and Systems Integration. The company offers IT equipment deployment services, including client products, enterprise products, clusters, and modular containers; and second-touch configuration services for OEM and end-user customers, such as adding software, hardware, or other features to end-user devices, bundling such devices with peripherals, pre-loading customer-determined application software, tagging, asset capture, and other fulfillment services. It also provides consulting, deployment, and maintenance and management services. In addition, the company is involved in procuring third-party hardware and software, as well as provides professional services. The company serves IT OEM equipment, technology, and service companies; private sector businesses; and government or commercial end users. The company was formerly known as Fortress International Group, Inc. and changed its name to TSS, Inc. in June 2013. TSS, Inc. was incorporated in 2004 and is based in Georgetown, Texas.

financial_summary: TSS, Inc. is a micro-cap technology business with a $189M market cap on $246M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +100% over the past three years and +24% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 40% against a 10% cost of capital — a 30-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $2M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.30× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -10.7% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 15× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.8% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
